rules.concept: Most English nouns form the plural by adding -s (or -es after s, x, z, ch, sh), so "box" becomes "boxes", not "boxs".
Some nouns have irregular plurals that are not formed with -s: "child → children", "mouse → mice", "man → men".
A possessive shows ownership with 's (singular) or s' (plural already ending in -s): "the boy's toy", "the boys' toys".
Verb endings must match their use: -s for third-person singular, -ed for past, -ing after be or as a gerund; spelling changes can apply ("run → running").
Many common verbs have irregular past-tense forms ("go → went", "take → took") that are not made by adding -ed.
With have/had, the past participle is required; irregular verbs often differ from the past tense ("had gone", not "had went").
Comparatives and superlatives use -er/-est for short adjectives and more/most for longer ones — not both ("taller" or "more tall", never "more taller").
An adverb is normally formed from an adjective with -ly ("happy → happily"); some adjectives already end in -ly and stay unchanged.
Reflexive pronouns end in -self/-selves and must match the subject ("himself", "yourself"), never non-standard forms like "hisself".
Homophones sound alike but differ in meaning and spelling: "its" (possessive) vs "it’s" (it is), "their"/"there"/"they’re".
A contraction replaces missing letters with an apostrophe ("do not → don’t", "I am → I’m"); dropping the apostrophe changes the word.
English spelling is not fully predictable, so some words must be learned ("receive", "necessary", "separate").
Numbers and measures have fixed patterns: hundred/thousand stay singular after a numeral ("two hundred", not "two hundreds"); units follow the noun.
A verb must agree in number with its subject: a singular subject takes a singular verb ("The boy goes"), a plural subject a plural verb.

rules.example: The boy with the bags go
rules.concept: Agreement ignores phrases between the subject and verb, so the verb matches the head noun, not the nearest noun ("The boy with the bags goes").
With subjects joined by "and" the verb is plural; with "or"/"nor" it agrees with the nearer subject ("Tom or Ann is").
In "there is/are", the verb agrees with the following noun, not with "there" ("There are books").
Collective and notional nouns can take a singular or plural verb depending on whether the group is treated as one unit or several members.
In questions the verb agrees with the subject and appears after the interrogative word ("Where are the books?").
Inside a relative clause the verb agrees with the relative pronoun’s antecedent ("the boys who play", not "who plays").
Indefinite pronouns like everyone, somebody, each take a singular verb ("Everyone has").
Quantified subjects agree according to the head: "each/a number of" patterns determine singular or plural ("Each of the boys is").
Demonstratives must match noun number: "this/that" with singular, "these/those" with plural ("these books").
Quantifiers pair with the right noun type: "much/little" with uncountable, "many/few" with countable ("less water", "fewer books").
A pronoun must match its antecedent in number and gender ("The girls lost their bags").
With correlatives (either...or, neither...nor) the verb agrees with the nearer subject ("Either he or I am").
A reflexive pronoun must refer back to the subject of the clause ("She hurt herself").
Use "an" before a vowel sound and "a" before a consonant sound ("an apple", "a house").
Singular countable nouns need a determiner in most contexts ("I saw a dog"), unless the meaning is generic or indefinite plural.
Do not add an article before activities, sports, or generic plurals ("She plays football", not "the football").
Use "the" for something already known or specific, and "a/an" for first mention or one of many.
Only one central determiner is allowed per noun phrase — do not stack them ("my book", not "the my book").
A determiner must modify a noun; it cannot stand alone without one ("the my" is incomplete).
Use "some" mainly in positive statements and "any" in questions and negatives ("I don’t have any money").
Distributive determiners match noun number and meaning: "each/every" + singular, "another" + singular, "other/all" + plural.
Uncountable nouns have no plural and take no "a/an" ("information", "advice"), unlike countable nouns ("a fact", "two facts").
When a noun modifies another noun it usually stays singular ("a ten-year plan", "a shoe shop").
Some nouns are plural-only ("scissors", "trousers") and some look plural but are singular ("the news is").

rules.example: Me go, between you and I
rules.concept: Pronouns change form by grammatical role: subject ("I", "he") vs object ("me", "him"), including after prepositions and "between".
In coordinated or compared phrases, keep the pronoun in the case the role requires ("He and I went", not "Me and him went").
A pronoun should refer clearly to one antecedent; if two nouns could be meant, the reference is ambiguous and should be rewritten.
Choose the relative pronoun by the antecedent: "who" for people, "which" for things, "that" for either in restrictive clauses.
Dummy "it"/"there" must be present where English requires a subject ("It is raining", not "Is raining").
A possessive determiner ("my") needs a following noun; a possessive pronoun ("mine") stands alone ("This is mine", not "This is my").
A reflexive pronoun cannot be the subject of a finite clause; use an ordinary pronoun ("I am happy", not "Myself am happy").
After an auxiliary or modal, use the required form: base form after modals ("can go"), past participle after have, -ing after be.
A main clause needs a finite verb (tensed and agreeing), not a bare -ing or infinitive with no auxiliary ("She goes to school").
English clauses need a verb, including the copula "be"; adjectives cannot stand alone as predicates ("She is very happy").
A passive is formed with be + past participle ("The house was built"), not the bare base form.
Intransitive verbs (happen, arrive, sleep) have no passive because they take no object ("It happened", not "It was happened").
Stative verbs (know, like, believe) describe states and are not normally used in the progressive ("I know", not "I am knowing").
Keep tense and logic consistent across a sentence or narrative ("He said he would come").
Verbs take the complements their meaning allows; some need no preposition ("discuss", not "discuss about").
Some verbs are followed by a gerund, some by an infinitive, and some by both with a change in meaning ("enjoy swimming").
After the infinitive marker "to" use the base form ("to go", not "to goes").
A phrasal verb keeps its particle next to it, and a pronoun object must go between verb and particle ("pick it up").
Modals take the bare base form and add no "-s" or "-ed" ("must go", not "must to go").
Yes/no and wh- questions invert the subject and auxiliary ("Where are you going?").
Standard English uses a single negative; use "any" rather than a second "no" ("I don’t have any money").
Imperatives use the base form with no subject and no "-s" ("Go!", not "Goes!").
In real conditionals use present tense in the if-clause, not "will" ("If I go, I will see him").
After "wish" and in the subjunctive, use the past or base form for hypotheticals ("I wish I were here").
Reported speech shifts tense and uses "tell + person" or "say + clause" ("She told me", not "She said me").
Causative and perception verbs take specific structures: "make/let + base", "have/get + past participle", "see + base/-ing".
Different verbs select different clause patterns ("suggest going", "advise someone to go"), so the complement must match the verb.
Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Use the adverb after an action verb ("runs quickly").
When several adjectives stack, English fixes their order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.
Adverbs of frequency and degree have preferred positions and usually cannot split a verb and its object.
Participial adjectives differ: "-ing" describes the cause ("boring"), "-ed" describes the feeler ("bored").
Degree words combine with the right adjective and position: "big enough", "very good", "too big" — not "enough big".
Form comparatives once: either -er/-est or more/most, and use "than" for comparison ("taller than").
English puts most modifiers before the noun; reversing the order ("the car red") is ungrammatical.
The preposition a verb or adjective takes is fixed by convention ("depend on", not "depend in").
Some verbs require a preposition to introduce their object ("listen to music", not "listen music").
Some verbs already include the meaning of the preposition, so adding one is wrong ("discuss the plan").
Adjective + preposition pairs are fixed ("interested in", "good at", "afraid of").
Time and place prepositions follow set patterns: "at" a point, "on" a day/date, "in" a period/area.
A preposition is followed by a noun or a gerund ("look forward to seeing"), not a bare infinitive.
A sentence needs at least one independent clause; a subordinate clause alone is a fragment ("Because I was late" cannot stand alone).
A finite clause needs a subject; leaving it out produces a fragment ("I went to school").

rules.example: I like tea she likes coffee
rules.concept: Two independent clauses cannot sit side by side without a conjunction or punctuation ("I like tea, but she likes coffee").
A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; use a conjunction, a semicolon, or a full stop.
Do not give the subject twice with a pronoun ("My brother went", not "My brother he went").
Statements use subject-before-verb order; inverted order belongs only to questions ("Yesterday I went").
A clause should carry exactly the words it needs; extras or omissions break the structure ("She is very happy").
Items in a list or comparison must share the same grammatical form ("to run and to swim", not "to run and swimming").
Correlative conjunctions come in fixed pairs; do not add a second connector ("Although X, Y" without "but").

rules.example: the man who I saw him
rules.concept: A relative clause already contains the role of the antecedent, so do not repeat it with a pronoun ("the man who I saw").
A modifier at the start of a sentence should describe the subject of the main clause ("Walking home, I saw the rain start").
Avoid redundant words that repeat meaning ("return", not "return back").
An embedded question keeps statement word order ("I wonder where he is").
Link clauses with the structure each connector requires ("because I wanted to see you").
Give the direct and indirect object in the standard order, or use the right preposition ("give me a book", "give a book to me").
Begin every sentence with a capital letter.
Capitalise proper nouns, the pronoun "I", and the names of days and months.
End a declarative or imperative sentence with a full stop, a question with "?" and a strong exclamation with "!".
Commas separate list items, mark introductory phrases, and set off non-essential clauses — but they cannot join two main clauses.
Apostrophes mark possession and contraction, not ordinary plurals ("the 1990s").
Quotation marks must be opened and closed around the exact words, with punctuation placed correctly.
Use hyphens to join compound modifiers before a noun ("a well-known author") and dashes for breaks in a sentence.
Use a colon to introduce a list or explanation and a semicolon to join closely related independent clauses.
Use single spaces between words and avoid accidental repeated words ("the the").
Follow consistent conventions for numbers, dates, and abbreviations within a text.
Confusable words sound or look alike but differ in meaning or part of speech ("affect" = verb, "effect" = noun).
Collocations are word partnerships fixed by convention ("make a decision", not "do a decision").
The tense must match the time expressed by adverbs such as "yesterday" ("Yesterday I went").
A verb’s meaning restricts what can be its subject or object ("The book eats" is impossible).
Some sentences have more than one possible structure; the intended meaning should be made explicit.
Register should match the situation: slang and casual forms do not belong in formal writing.
First-language patterns can produce errors in English ("I am agree" from "estoy de acuerdo"); use the English structure.

rules.example: I was tired, however I slept
rules.concept: Connectors express a specific logical relation, so the one chosen must match the meaning ("I was tired, so I slept").
